content: Isosorbide is a medication prescribed to prevent or treat chest pain (angina). It functions by relaxing the blood vessels supplying the heart, thereby increasing the flow of blood and oxygen to the heart. This medication may also be prescribed for other uses; consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information. Isosorbide is available in various forms, including regular tablets, sublingual tablets, chewable tablets, extended-release tablets, and extended-release capsules, all of which are taken orally. Regular tablets are typically taken every six hours. Extended-release tablets are usually taken once or twice daily, while extended-release capsules are taken every 8 to 12 hours. It is important not to crush, chew, or divide extended-release tablets or capsules. Chewable tablets may be used every 2 to 3 hours to prevent chest pain. Always follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Take isosorbide exactly as directed, without altering the dose or frequency unless instructed by your doctor. Isosorbide helps control chest pain but does not cure it. Continue taking the medication even if you feel well, and do not stop taking it without consulting your doctor, as abrupt discontinuation may cause chest pain. Prolonged use of isosorbide can lead to reduced effectiveness, a phenomenon known as tolerance. If your angina attacks become more frequent, last longer, or are more severe, contact your doctor immediately. If you are using sublingual or chewable tablets for acute chest pain, carry them with you at all times. If chest pain is not relieved within 5 to 10 minutes after taking a dose, take another dose. If pain persists after taking three doses at 5to 10-minute intervals over 15 to 30 minutes, seek emergency medical assistance or go to a hospital emergency department. During an angina attack, sit down. For chewable tablets, chew thoroughly before swallowing. For sublingual tablets, place one under your tongue or between your cheek and gum and allow it to dissolve without swallowing. Avoid swallowing saliva frequently until the tablet has dissolved. Isosorbide tablets may also be used in combination with other medications to treat congestive heart failure. Discuss the potential risks of using this medication for your condition with your doctor. Before taking isosorbide, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to isosorbide, nitroglycerin products, or any other drugs. Also, disclose any other medications, supplements, or vitamins you are taking, especially erectile dysfunction medications like sildenafil (Viagra), tadalafil (Cialis), or vardenafil (Levitra). Inform your doctor if you have or have ever had anemia, glaucoma, or recent head trauma. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, notify your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking isosorbide, contact your doctor immediately. If you are undergoing surgery, including dental surgery, inform your healthcare provider that you are taking isosorbide. Be aware that this medication may cause drowsiness or dizziness, so avoid driving or operating machinery until you know how it affects you. Additionally, inform your doctor if you consume large amounts of alcohol regularly, as alcohol can exacerbate the side effects of isosorbide. Take isosorbide tablets on an empty stomach, at least one hour before or two hours after meals, with a full glass of water. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one. Common side effects of isosorbide include headache, rash, dizziness, upset stomach, and flushing (a sensation of warmth). If these symptoms are severe or persistent, inform your doctor. Serious side effects, such as blurred vision, dry mouth, chest pain, or fainting, require immediate medical attention. If you experience a serious side effect, you or your doctor can report it to the FDA's MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program. Store isosorbide in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture (not in the bathroom). Sublingual and chewable tablets should remain in their original container and should not be opened until needed. Do not use tablets that are more than 12 months old. Dispose of outdated or unneeded medication properly, and consult your pharmacist for guidance on disposal. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call 911 immediately. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory. Regular and extended-release isosorbide tablets or capsules should not be used for acute angina attacks. Continue using sublingual or chewable tablets to relieve chest pain that has already started. If headaches persist, consult your doctor about taking acetaminophen. Do not take aspirin or other headache medications while using isosorbide unless directed by your doctor. Sublingual tablets may cause a sweet, tingling sensation when placed under the tongue; this is not an indicator of drug strength, and the absence of tingling does not mean the drug is ineffective. Do not share your medication with others. Consult your pharmacist if you have questions about refilling your prescription.
